query: Earlier studies reported high hardness and compressive strength in AlCrCuFeNiTi, CuFeNiMnTi, and low-density AlCrFeTiX high-entropy alloys. However, some AlCrFeTiX alloys were brittle at 25 °C, and AlCrFeTiCo showed only 1.8% plastic strain at 600 °C. Because these findings concern different alloy systems, they do not explain the deformation behavior or the relatively low hardness and strength of equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in its simple solid-solution state, despite its favorable plasticity and machinability. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs this combination of deformation, hardness, and strength and why? Define a controlled comparison that would distinguish the proposed explanation, predict observations relative to the starting alloy, state the composition, state, temperature, and loading limits of the hypothesis, identify the prior evidence supporting its premise, and specify results that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The relatively low hardness and strength of equimolar (or nearly equimolar) CoCrFeNiTi, despite its excellent plasticity and machinability, is governed by its microstructure being a simple solid solution that lacks nanoscale precipitates. In the absence of these strengthening features, dislocations move relatively freely, resulting in good ductility but a lower resistance to plastic flow (i.e. lower hardness and yield strength).
generation.material_initial_state: Equimolar or near‐equimolar CoCrFeNiTi produced as a single‐phase solid solution (with, for example, an FCC or BCC structure) without any secondary precipitates.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled thermal aging (or annealing) treatment designed to induce a uniform dispersion of nanoscale precipitates within the solid-solution matrix. The treatment should be carried out at a temperature selected to promote precipitation (e.g., near 600 °C) for a time sufficient to allow nucleation and growth of fine precipitates without dissolving the matrix.
generation.conditions: Material: equimolar CoCrFeNiTi; Processing: as-cast simple solid solution versus identical alloy subjected to post-casting thermal aging at a designated temperature (e.g., ~600 °C) for a controlled time under an inert or vacuum atmosphere; Evaluation: mechanical testing (e.g., compression tests) at room temperature and at elevated temperatures (e.g., 600 °C) while keeping loading rate and other testing parameters controlled.
generation.structural_mediator: The emergence of nanoscale precipitates (or fine secondary phases) within the solid-solution matrix.
generation.mechanism: The formation of nanoscale precipitates will act as obstacles to dislocation motion (via precipitate strengthening mechanisms), thereby increasing hardness and yield strength. In the as-cast, precipitation-free simple solid solution, dislocations glide with fewer impediments, which confers excellent ductility and machinability but results in relatively lower hardness and strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline as-cast CoCrFeNiTi, the thermally aged (precipitation-engineered) sample will exhibit higher hardness and increased yield (or compressive) strength. The magnitude of improvement is expected to be qualitatively significant, although the precise quantitative change is uncertain.
generation.baseline: Equimolar (or near equimolar) CoCrFeNiTi in the simple solid-solution state as produced by direct casting without additional aging treatment.
generation.boundary: The alloy’s composition (equimolar CoCrFeNiTi) and its simple solid-solution state are fixed. Mechanical testing should be performed at room temperature and up to 600 °C with controlled loading conditions, ensuring that the only variable is the presence or absence of thermally induced nanoscale precipitates.
generation.uncertainty: While the qualitative effect (increased hardness and strength due to precipitation strengthening) is expected, the exact magnitude of hardness and yield strength improvement and the corresponding reduction in ductility are not precisely predictable without experimental calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of equimolar CoCrFeNiTi specimens — one set maintained in the as-cast simple solid-solution state and a matched set subjected to a controlled thermal aging treatment (e.g., aging at ~600 °C for a predetermined time under inert atmosphere) to induce nanoscale precipitates. Characterize the microstructure by TEM and XRD to confirm precipitate formation in the aged set. Then, conduct standardized mechanical tests (e.g., compressive or tensile tests at room temperature and 600 °C) on both sets.
measurements: Microstructural analysis (precipitate size, distribution and volume fraction by TEM/XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermally aged samples do not show a statistically significant increase in hardness and yield (compressive) strength compared to the as-cast samples – or if no nanoscale precipitates can be detected despite the aging treatment – then the hypothesis that the lack of precipitates is responsible for the relatively low hardness and strength is falsified.

In this study, the mechanical behavior of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high entropy alloy at small length scales was investigated for fundamental understanding of phase-specific contribution to the bulk mechanical response. The main conclusions are as follows:The as-cast microstructure consisted of eutectic lamellae of: (a) L12 phase rich in Fe, Co, Cr and (b) B2 phase rich in Ni and Al. The average grain size of the cast alloy was ~100 μm. The B2 phase consisted of Cr-rich precipitates with disordered BCC structure and average size of ~20 nm.The AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high entropy alloy showed excellent combination of strength and ductility in tensile and compression loading. In tensile loading, it showed a yield strength of 750 ± 24 MPa, ultimate tensile strength of 1165 ± 20 MPa and elongation of ~18%. In compressive loading, the yield strength was 517 ± 7 MPa, ultimate compressive strength was 1863 ± 12 MPa, and plasticity of ~34.3%. The fracture morphologies confirmed brittle mode for B2 phase and ductile mode for L12 phase.The B2 phase showed higher hardness and slightly lower modulus than L12 phase.
